constraints.meaning: nums1 already has room for every value. The first m slots are real values; the last n slots are placeholder zeros.
constraints.impact: No new array is needed. The free space sits at the end, so filling nums1 from the back never overwrites a value we still need.

constraints.meaning: nums2 holds exactly the n values to merge in.
constraints.impact: The loop can stop as soon as all n values of nums2 are placed.

constraints.meaning: Either array can be empty: m = 0 means nums1 has only placeholders, n = 0 means there is nothing to merge.
constraints.impact: The code must handle p1 < 0 (nums1 used up) and n = 0 (loop never runs) without reading outside the arrays.

constraints.meaning: At most 200 values in total, and never zero.
constraints.impact: Even O(n²) would be fast here. The O(m + n) merge is what interviewers expect, and the follow-up asks for it.

constraints.meaning: Negative values and real zeros can appear.
constraints.impact: Values fit in int. A 0 inside the first m slots is a real value, so you cannot spot the free slots by looking for zeros: use m.

constraints.text: Both arrays sorted in non-decreasing order (statement)
constraints.meaning: Each array is already in order; duplicates are allowed.
constraints.impact: The largest remaining value is always at the end of one of the two arrays, so one comparison per slot is enough.

bruteForce.summary: copy nums2 into the empty tail of nums1, then sort the whole array: O((m+n) log(m+n)) with a library sort. It throws away the fact that both parts are already sorted. The code below sorts with insertion sort so each comparison can be counted.
